claim: In most vertebrates, the upper digestive tract is composed of muscularized jaws linked to the esophagus that permits food ingestion and swallowing.
source: In most vertebrates, the upper digestive tract is composed of muscularized jaws linked to the esophagus that permits food ingestion and swallowing.
evidence: This is a statement of established anatomical knowledge about vertebrate digestive systems.

claim: Masticatory and esophagus striated muscles share a common cardiopharyngeal mesoderm (CPM) origin.
source: Masticatory and esophagus striated muscles (ESM) share a common cardiopharyngeal mesoderm (CPM) origin
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work and is part of the established understanding of muscle development.

claim: ESM are unusual among striated muscles as they are established in the absence of a primary skeletal muscle scaffold.
source: however ESM are unusual among striated muscles as they are established in the absence of a primary skeletal muscle scaffold.
evidence: This is a key observation about ESM development that distinguishes them from other striated muscles.

claim: Tbx1 and Isl1 are required cell-autonomously for myogenic specification of ESM progenitors.
source: Using mouse chimeras, we show that the transcription factors Tbx1 and Isl1 are required cell-autonomously for myogenic specification of ESM progenitors.
evidence: This claim is supported by the chimera experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: MET/HGF signaling is required for antero-posterior migration of esophagus muscle progenitors.
source: Further, genetic loss-of-function and pharmacological studies point to MET/HGF signaling for antero-posterior migration of esophagus muscle progenitors
evidence: This is supported by genetic and pharmacological experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: Hgf ligand is expressed in adjacent smooth muscle cells.
source: where Hgf ligand is expressed in adjacent smooth muscle cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated by in situ hybridization experiments shown in the manuscript.

claim: A Tbx1-Isl1-Met genetic hierarchy uniquely regulates esophagus myogenesis.
source: Our findings establish a Tbx1-Isl1-Met genetic hierarchy that uniquely regulates esophagus myogenesis
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Evolution of vertebrates has been marked by the emergence of muscularized jaws that transitioned them from filter feeders to active predators.
source: Evolution of vertebrates has been marked by the emergence of muscularized jaws that transitioned them from filter feeders to active predators (Glenn Northcutt, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Glenn Northcutt, 2005.

claim: Muscles of the trunk originate from the segmented somites.
source: Muscles of the trunk originate from the segmented somites
evidence: This is established knowledge in developmental biology.

claim: Head muscles arise independently from the cardiopharyngeal mesoderm (CPM) located anterior to the somites.
source: whereas head muscles arise independently from the cardiopharyngeal mesoderm (CPM) located anterior to the somites (Diogo et al., 2015; Sambasivan et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Diogo et al., 2015 and Sambasivan et al., 2011.

claim: The specification of head and trunk muscles involves divergent genetic regulatory networks to activate the bHLH myogenic regulatory factors (MRFs) Myf5, Mrf4, Myod and Myogenin.
source: The specification of head and trunk muscles involves divergent genetic regulatory networks, to activate the bHLH myogenic regulatory factors (MRFs) Myf5, Mrf4, Myod and Myogenin that play crucial roles in governing striated muscle cell fate and differentiation (Comai et al., 2014; Kassar-Duchossoy et al., 2005; Rudnicki et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Somitic myogenic progenitors are regulated primarily by the Pax3/Pax7 paired/homeodomain genes and Myf5 that act genetically upstream of Myod.
source: While somitic myogenic progenitors are regulated primarily by the Pax3/Pax7 paired/homeodomain genes and Myf5 that act genetically upstream of Myod (Kassar-Duchossoy et al., 2005; Relaix et al., 2005; Tajbakhsh et al., 1997)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Cardiopharyngeal mesoderm progenitors are regulated by a Pax3-independent regulatory network.
source: cardiopharyngeal mesoderm progenitors, that colonize pharyngeal arches and form craniofacial and some neck muscles, are regulated by a Pax3-independent regulatory network (Heude et al., 2018; Sambasivan et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Heude et al., 2018 and Sambasivan et al., 2011.

claim: CPM progenitors specified by Tbx1 and Isl1 genes are bipotent as they form branchiomeric subsets of head/neck muscles as well as the second heart field.
source: CPM progenitors specified by Tbx1 and Isl1 genes are bipotent as they form branchiomeric subsets of head/neck muscles as well as the second heart field (Diogo et al., 2015; Kelly et al., 2004; Lescroart et al., 2015; Sambasivan et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Tbx1 acts together with Myf5 to assure myogenic fate.
source: Tbx1 acts together with Myf5 to assure myogenic fate (Harel et al., 2009; Kelly et al., 2004; Nathan et al., 2008; Sambasivan et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: In Tbx1-null embryos, the first pharyngeal arch is hypoplastic and posterior pharyngeal arches do not form.
source: In Tbx1-null embryos, the first pharyngeal arch is hypoplastic and posterior pharyngeal arches do not form, resulting in variably penetrant defects of masticatory muscles and absence of muscles derived from more posterior arches including those of the larynx and esophagus (Gopalakrishnan et al., 2015; Heude et al., 2018; Kelly et al., 2004; Lescroart et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Tbx1 exerts cell-autonomous and non-autonomous roles.
source: Tbx1 exerts cell-autonomous and non-autonomous roles as conditional deletion of Tbx1 in CPM and pharyngeal endoderm phenocopies the pharyngeal arch and cardiac outflow tract phenotype of the null mutant (Arnold et al., 2006; Kelly et al., 2004; Zhang, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Isl1-null mutants exhibit early embryonic lethality by E10.5 with cardiac deficiencies.
source: On the other hand, the functional role of Isl1 in CPM specification remains unknown due to early embryonic lethality of Isl1-null mutants (by E10.5) that exhibit cardiac deficiencies (Cai et al., 2003; Harel et al., 2009; Nathan et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: CPM progenitors generate diverse myogenic subpopulations at the transition zone between head and trunk.
source: Recent studies by us and others showed that CPM progenitors generate diverse myogenic subpopulations at the transition zone between head and trunk (Diogo et al., 2015; Gopalakrishnan et al., 2015; Heude et al., 2018; Lescroart et al., 2015; Schubert et al., 2019; Tabler et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to recent work.

claim: Esophagus striated muscles arise from the CPM.
source: We have previously shown that esophagus striated muscles (ESM) arise from the CPM and exhibit several features that are distinct from other striated muscles in the organism.
evidence: This is based on previous work by the authors.

claim: ESM formation initiates in the fetus, thus embryonic myogenesis which generates primary myofibers that act as scaffolds for secondary (fetal) myofibers does not take place.
source: Notably, ESM formation initiates in the fetus, thus embryonic myogenesis which generates primary myofibers that act as scaffolds for secondary (fetal) myofibers does not take place (Gopalakrishnan et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Gopalakrishnan et al., 2015.

claim: The mammalian esophagus is composed of both striated and smooth muscle layers, which have a distinct developmental origin.
source: The mammalian esophagus is composed of both striated and smooth muscle layers, which have a distinct developmental origin (Gopalakrishnan et al., 2015; Krauss et al., 2016; Rishniw et al., 2003; Zhao and Dhoot, 2000a).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Postnatal maturation of the esophagus striated musculature involves proximo-distal replacement of smooth muscle by as yet elusive mechanisms.
source: Postnatal maturation of the esophagus striated musculature involves proximo-distal replacement of smooth muscle by as yet elusive mechanisms (Krauss et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Krauss et al., 2016.

claim: Perturbations of esophagus function lead to dysphagia and other pathophysiological disorders that impair swallowing and transfer of bolus to the stomach.
source: Perturbations of esophagus function lead to dysphagia and other pathophysiological disorders that impair swallowing and transfer of bolus to the stomach (Sheehan, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sheehan, 2008.

claim: In Tbx1-null embryos, Isl1-derived myogenic cells fail to seed the anterior esophagus.
source: In Tbx1-null embryos, Isl1-derived myogenic cells fail to seed the anterior esophagus, suggesting that Tbx1 acts genetically upstream of Isl1 in ESM progenitors (Gopalakrishnan et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Gopalakrishnan et al., 2015.

claim: CPM-derived progenitors are seeded at the bottom of the oropharyngeal cavity by E13.5.
source: Initially, CPM-derived progenitors are seeded at the bottom of the oropharyngeal cavity by E13.5.
evidence: This is a description of the developmental timeline based on observations.

claim: Isl1-derived ESM progenitors colonize the esophagus by posterior migration and differentiation until the third week of postnatal growth.
source: Then, Isl1-derived ESM progenitors colonize the esophagus by posterior migration and differentiation until the third week of postnatal growth (Gopalakrishnan et al., 2015; Romer et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gopalakrishnan et al., 2015 and Romer et al., 2013.

claim: MET receptor is expressed in migratory progenitors.
source: This process is regulated by the tyrosine kinase receptor MET, expressed in migratory progenitors, and its ligand Scatter Factor/Hepatocyte Growth Factor (SF/HGF) expressed in mesenchymal cells along the migratory route (Bladt et al., 1995; Brand-Saberi et al., 1996; Dietrich et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: SF/HGF is expressed in mesenchymal cells along the migratory route.
source: This process is regulated by the tyrosine kinase receptor MET, expressed in migratory progenitors, and its ligand Scatter Factor/Hepatocyte Growth Factor (SF/HGF) expressed in mesenchymal cells along the migratory route (Bladt et al., 1995; Brand-Saberi et al., 1996; Dietrich et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Knockout of either Met or Hgf in mice results in the absence of hypaxial muscles including limb muscles, diaphragm and the tip of the tongue.
source: Knockout of either Met or Hgf in mice results in the absence of hypaxial muscles including limb muscles, diaphragm and the tip of the tongue (Bladt et al., 1995; Dietrich et al., 1999; Maina et al., 1996; Prunotto et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Second (hyoid) arch-derived muscles are affected in Met KO mice.
source: Although second (hyoid) arch-derived muscles are affected in Met KO mice (Prunotto et al., 2004), a role for MET/HGF signaling in establishing other CPM muscles including those in the larynx and esophagus has not been reported.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Prunotto et al., 2004.

claim: MET/HGF signaling is critical for ESM patterning, but not for the establishment of adjacent laryngeal muscles.
source: Using genetic loss-of-function and pharmacological inhibition approaches, we show that MET/HGF signaling is critical for ESM patterning, but not for the establishment of adjacent laryngeal muscles.
evidence: This is a key finding from the experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: All Tbx1-null chimeric embryos analyzed between E14.5 and E15.5 lacked thymus glands.
source: All Tbx1-null chimeric embryos analyzed between E14.5 and E15.5 lacked thymus glands (n=9)
evidence: This is a direct observation from the chimera experiments.

claim: 77% of Tbx1-null chimeric embryos were edemic and lacked the outer ear pinna.
source: and 77% of them were edemic and lacked the outer ear pinna indicating that the contribution of Isl1lacZ ES cells (Tbx1wildtype) was not extensive enough to fully rescue the Tbx1 knockout phenotype
evidence: This is a direct observation from the chimera experiments.

claim: 5/5 chimeric Tbx1-/- embryos analyzed contained β-gal+ cells in the esophagus.
source: Whole mount X-gal staining showed that 5/5 chimeric Tbx1-/- embryos analyzed contained β-gal+ cells in the esophagus
evidence: This is a direct observation from the chimera experiments.

claim: β-gal+ cells were present within the smooth muscle layers of the esophagus of Tbx1-null embryos (8/8 chimeras analyzed).
source: We observed that β-gal+ cells were present within the smooth muscle layers of the esophagus of Tbx1-null embryos (8/8 chimeras analyzed), and colocalised within Tnnt3+/Tuj1- (myogenic/non-neurogenic) cells
evidence: This is a direct observation from the chimera experiments.

claim: Isl1lacZ ES cells can colonize an overall Tbx1-null esophageal environment.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that Isl1lacZ ES cells can colonize an overall Tbx1-null esophageal environment suggesting cell autonomous potential of Tbx1+/Isl1+ progenitors to seed and pattern the ESM.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the chimera experiments.

claim: Isl1 is expressed in peripheral neurons.
source: Apart from its expression in ESM progenitors, Isl1 is expressed in peripheral neurons (Pfaff et al., 1996) and in the pharyngeal and esophageal epithelium (Cai et al., 2003; Harel et al., 2009; Nathan et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Isl1 is expressed in the pharyngeal and esophageal epithelium.
source: Apart from its expression in ESM progenitors, Isl1 is expressed in peripheral neurons (Pfaff et al., 1996) and in the pharyngeal and esophageal epithelium (Cai et al., 2003; Harel et al., 2009; Nathan et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Macroscopic examination of chimeras at E16.5 did not reveal obvious developmental defects in Isl1-null chimeras compared to controls.
source: Macroscopic examination of chimeras at E16.5 did not reveal obvious developmental defects in Isl1-null chimeras compared to controls.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the chimera experiments.

claim: GFP+ Isl1-derived CPM cells contribute to the esophagus myogenic population (Myod/Myog/Tnnt3+), but not to the esophagus smooth muscle (SMA+) and striated muscle of tongue.
source: For reference, contribution of β-gal+ ES-derived cells was compared with Isl1 lineage tracing (Isl1Cre/+;R26mT/mG/+ embryos), whereby GFP+ Isl1-derived CPM cells contribute to the esophagus myogenic population (Myod/Myog/Tnnt3+), but not to the esophagus smooth muscle (SMA+) and striated muscle of tongue that develop in an Isl1-independent context
evidence: This is demonstrated by lineage tracing experiments shown in Figure 1C-E.

claim: In control chimeras, β-gal+ cells gave rise to both SMA+ (31–46%) and Myod/Myog+ populations (25–43%).
source: In the esophagus of control chimeras, β-gal+ cells gave rise to both SMA+ (31–46%) and Myod/Myog+ populations (25–43%)
evidence: This is quantified data from the chimera experiments shown in Figure 1L.

claim: Isl1-null/β-gal+ cells were excluded from the esophagus Myod/Myog+ cells.
source: In contrast, Isl1-null/β-gal+ cells were excluded from the esophagus Myod/Myog+ cells
evidence: This is quantified data from the chimera experiments shown in Figure 1L.

claim: Isl1-null cells contributed to esophagus smooth muscle and tongue myogenic cells in both Isl1-null and control chimeras to a similar extent.
source: whereas they contributed to a similar extent to esophagus smooth muscle and tongue myogenic cells in both Isl1-null and control chimeras.
evidence: This is quantified data from the chimera experiments shown in Figure 1L-M.

claim: Isl1 is necessary cell-autonomously for progenitor cells to adopt a myogenic cell fate in the esophagus.
source: These results show that Isl1 is necessary cell-autonomously for progenitor cells to adopt a myogenic cell fate in the esophagus
evidence: This is the conclusion drawn from the chimera experiments.

claim: ESM development occurs in a biphasic mode, with initial seeding of Isl1-positive myogenic progenitors at the anterior esophagus followed by anterior-posterior migration and differentiation that proceeds to postnatal stages.
source: ESM development occurs in a biphasic mode, with initial seeding of Isl1-positive myogenic progenitors at the anterior esophagus followed by anterior-posterior migration and differentiation that proceeds to postnatal stages (Gopalakrishnan et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Gopalakrishnan et al., 2015.

claim: Isl1 is known to maintain cells in an undifferentiated state in branchiomeric muscle progenitors.
source: Isl1 is known to maintain cells in an undifferentiated state in branchiomeric muscle progenitors (Cai et al., 2003; Nathan et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Isl1 and Myf5 transcripts were detected in the anterior, middle and posterior esophagus as ESM progenitors colonize the structure from E15.5 to 3 weeks postnatally.
source: Isl1 and Myf5 transcripts were detected in the anterior, middle and posterior esophagus as ESM progenitors colonize the structure from E15.5 to 3 weeks postnatally
evidence: This is demonstrated by RT-qPCR analysis shown in Figure 2A-C.

claim: Isl1 expression was also detected in the stomach.
source: Isl1 expression was also detected in the stomach, as already described for the gastric epithelium (Das and May, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Das and May, 2011.

claim: Isl1 was expressed in Pax7-nGFP+ esophagus progenitors.
source: Isl1 was expressed in Pax7-nGFP+ esophagus progenitors, whereas expression was low or undetectable in those isolated from the masseter at all stages analyzed.
evidence: This is demonstrated by RT-qPCR analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Isl1 expression is maintained in myogenic progenitors throughout ESM development.
source: Therefore, Isl1 expression is maintained in myogenic progenitors throughout ESM development.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the RT-qPCR data.

claim: Pax7-nGFP+ ESM progenitors showed transcript abundance of Met at fetal stages and lower expression levels postnatally when ESM colonization was complete.
source: Notably, Pax7-nGFP+ ESM progenitors showed transcript abundance of Met at fetal stages and lower expression levels postnatally when ESM colonization was complete
evidence: This is demonstrated by RT-qPCR analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Met levels were higher in the anterior esophagus portion at E13.5 and E15.5, and become upregulated also in the middle part by E17.5.
source: Along the anterior-posterior axis, Met levels were higher in the anterior esophagus portion at E13.5 and E15.5, and become upregulated also in the middle part by E17.5
evidence: This is demonstrated by RT-qPCR analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Hgf levels seemed initially constant along the esophagus length at E13.5, but appeared downregulated anteriorly in parallel with SMA at later stages.
source: Hgf levels seemed initially constant along the esophagus length at E13.5, but appeared downregulated anteriorly in parallel with SMA at later stages
evidence: This is demonstrated by RT-qPCR analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: MET/HGF signaling might be implicated in A-P migration of ESM progenitors from fetal to postnatal stages.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that MET/HGF signaling might be implicated in A-P migration of ESM progenitors from fetal to postnatal stages.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the expression data.

claim: MetD/D and Hgf-null fetuses showed absence of striated muscles in the esophagus.
source: Interestingly, MetD/D and Hgf-null fetuses showed absence of striated muscles in the esophagus, while the smooth muscle layers and lumen epithelium appeared unaffected
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunostaining shown in Figure 2F-K.

claim: The smooth muscle layers and lumen epithelium appeared unaffected in MetD/D and Hgf-null fetuses.
source: Interestingly, MetD/D and Hgf-null fetuses showed absence of striated muscles in the esophagus, while the smooth muscle layers and lumen epithelium appeared unaffected
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunostaining shown in Figure 2F-K.

claim: MetD/D and Hgf-null mutants lacked limb muscles typical of the MetD/D and Hgf-null phenotypes.
source: As expected, these mutants lacked limb muscles typical of the MetD/D and Hgf-null phenotypes
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunostaining shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A-F.

claim: RT-qPCR analysis in the esophagus and limb of Met mutants at E15.5 revealed a decrease but not loss of Isl1 and Myf5 expression compared to absence of Pax7 and Myf5 observed at limb level.
source: However, RT-qPCR analysis in the esophagus and limb of Met mutants at E15.5 revealed a decrease but not loss of Isl1 and Myf5 expression compared to absence of Pax7 and Myf5 observed at limb level
evidence: This is demonstrated by RT-qPCR analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2G.

claim: The number of Isl1+ cells in the upper esophagus of E13.5 controls and Met mutants was not significantly different.
source: Analysis on tissue sections revealed that the number of Isl1+ cells in the upper esophagus of E13.5 controls and Met mutants was not significantly different (n = 3)
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-A''.

claim: The myogenic progenitors had seeded the anterior esophagus in mutant embryos similarly to controls at E13.5.
source: Thus, the myogenic progenitors had seeded the anterior esophagus in mutant embryos similarly to controls at this initial stage.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the quantification of Isl1+ cells.

claim: Myf5+ myogenic cells were present in the anterior-most portion of the esophagus in the Met mutant at E15.5 and E17.5.
source: Moreover, analysis of MetD/+ ; Myf5nlacZ/+ (control) and MetD/D ; Myf5nlacZ/+ (mutant) esophagi at E15.5 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,C) and E17.5 (Figure 3D,E; Figure 3—figure supplement 1D,E) showed that Myf5+ myogenic cells were also present in the anterior-most portion of the esophagus in the mutant, whereas colonization had proceeded posteriorly only in the controls.
evidence: This is demonstrated by whole mount immunostaining shown in Figure 3D,E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B-E.

claim: The neuronal and smooth muscle lineages were present and patterned in Met mutants.
source: Of note, the neuronal and smooth muscle lineages were present and patterned in mutants
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunostaining shown in Figure 3D,E.

claim: Very few mononucleated mGFP+ cells were detected between the residual myofibers in the anterior-most part of the esophagus in the Met mutant.
source: However, very few mononucleated mGFP+ cells were detected between the residual myofibers in the anterior-most part of the esophagus in the Met mutant
evidence: This is demonstrated by lineage tracing shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The adjacent Isl1-derived laryngeal and pharyngeal muscles were unaffected in the Met-null fetuses.
source: Strikingly, the adjacent Isl1-derived laryngeal and pharyngeal muscles were unaffected in the Met-null fetuses
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunostaining shown in Figure 3C,C',D-G and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B-E.

claim: MET/HGF loss of function affect only a subset of posterior CPM-derived progenitors that are critical for colonization of the esophagus but not for the development of adjacent Isl1-lineage-derived muscles.
source: Therefore, these observations indicate that MET/HGF loss of function affect only a subset of posterior CPM-derived progenitors that are critical for colonization of the esophagus but not for the development of adjacent Isl1-lineage-derived muscles.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observations in Met mutants.

claim: Met acts downstream of Isl1 in the molecular hierarchy of ESM formation.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that Met acts downstream of Isl1 in the molecular hierarchy of ESM formation
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the genetic analysis.

claim: MET/HGF signaling is not implicated in initial seeding of Isl1-derived progenitors in the anterior esophagus, but rather during the second phase of myogenic migration.
source: and that MET/HGF signaling is not implicated in initial seeding of Isl1-derived progenitors in the anterior esophagus, but rather during the second phase of myogenic migration.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the timing of defects in Met mutants.

claim: Isl1+ progenitors in the upper esophagus were not apoptotic at E13.5 in Met mutant embryos.
source: TUNEL analysis in E13.5 controls and Met mutants revealed that Isl1+ progenitors in the upper esophagus were not apoptotic at this stage
evidence: This is demonstrated by TUNEL assay shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,A'.

claim: On control static cultures and time-lapse imaging, a mGFP+ mononucleated cell front remained throughout the entire culture period.
source: On control static cultures (followed up to 24 hr) and time-lapse imaging (up to 14 hr), we observed a mGFP+ mononucleated cell front that remained throughout the entire culture period
evidence: This is demonstrated by explant culture experiments shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Time-lapse movies showed that mGFP+ cells explored the esophagus scaffold repeatedly changing their direction of migration, but had a net movement posteriorly towards the stomach.
source: In addition, time-lapse movies showed that mGFP+ cells explored the esophagus scaffold repeatedly changing their direction of migration, but had a net movement posteriorly towards the stomach
evidence: This is demonstrated by time-lapse imaging shown in Figure 4E and Figure 4—video 1.

claim: Upon addition of MET inhibitors, mGFP+ cells progressed less towards the posterior end.
source: In contrast, upon addition of MET inhibitors, mGFP+ cells progressed less towards the posterior end
evidence: This is demonstrated by time-lapse imaging shown in Figure 4C,D and Figure 4—videos 2 and 3.

claim: In presence of MET inhibitors, mGFP+ cells had a reduced velocity, displacement, efficiency, and net velocity compared to control cultures.
source: Quantification of migration parameters revealed that in presence of MET inhibitors, mGFP+ cells had a reduced velocity, displacement, efficiency, and net velocity compared to control cultures
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification shown in Figure 4I-L.

claim: mGFP+ fibers appeared rapidly in the inhibitor treated cultures in positions where the cell density appeared higher.
source: Interestingly, mGFP+ fibers appeared rapidly in the inhibitor treated cultures in positions where the cell density appeared higher
evidence: This is demonstrated by time-lapse imaging shown in Figure 4C,D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Myogenic cells in the esophagus of MetD/D mutant embryos have a proliferation rate that was one third of controls at E14.5.
source: Analysis of E14.5 and E15.5 embryos showed that myogenic cells in the esophagus of MetD/D mutant embryos have a proliferation rate that was one third of controls (45,6% for Ctrl; 12,5% for Mutant at E14.5
evidence: This is demonstrated by EdU labelling shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Myogenic cells in the esophagus of MetD/D mutant embryos have a higher predisposition to differentiation as assessed by Myogenin expression at E14.5.
source: and a higher predisposition to differentiation as assessed by Myogenin expression (33% for Ctrl; 66% for Mutant at E14.5
evidence: This is demonstrated by Myogenin immunostaining shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claim: MET/HGF signaling promotes A-P migration of ESM myogenic progenitors during fetal development.
source: In summary, our ex vivo and in vivo analyzes indicate that MET/HGF signaling promotes A-P migration of ESM myogenic progenitors during fetal development
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the ex vivo and in vivo experiments.

claim: MET/HGF signaling possibly maintains Isl1-derived progenitors in an undifferentiated state once they have colonized the upper esophagus.
source: and possibly maintains Isl1-derived progenitors in an undifferentiated state once they have colonized the upper esophagus.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the differentiation data.

claim: Hgf transcripts were present along the entire length of the esophagus, preceeding and following the myogenic cell front, at the seeding stage (E13.5) and during myogenic migration (E14.5).
source: Whole mount in situ hybridization (RNAscope) on Isl1Cre;R26mT/mG embryos showed that Hgf transcripts were present along the entire length of the esophagus, preceeding and following the myogenic cell front, at the seeding stage (E13.5) and during myogenic migration (E14.5)
evidence: This is demonstrated by whole mount in situ hybridization shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Hgf was expressed adjacent to mGFP+ cells in a bilayered concentric pattern overlapping with the smooth muscle layers of the esophagus.
source: In situ hybridization on sections revealed that Hgf was expressed adjacent to mGFP+ cells in a bilayered concentric pattern overlapping with the smooth muscle layers of the esophagus
evidence: This is demonstrated by in situ hybridization shown in Figure 5A,B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Initially at E14.5, myogenic cells colonized exclusively the outer smooth muscle layer.
source: Initially at E14.5, although a bilayered pattern of Hgf is observed, myogenic cells colonized exclusively the outer smooth muscle layer
evidence: This is demonstrated by in situ hybridization shown in Figure 5A.

claim: At E16.5, expression of Hgf appeared to be downregulated anteriorly in the outer layer.
source: At E16.5, expression of Hgf appeared to be downregulated anteriorly in the outer layer (level 1; Figure 5—figure supplement 1E), concomitant with the described regression of smooth muscle in the anterior esophagus from late fetal stages (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–C) (Zhao and Dhoot, 2000a).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in situ hybridization shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E.

claim: At E16.5, myogenic cells started to colonize the inner layer anteriorly, and this corresponded to downregulation of Hgf expression in the outer layer.
source: At this stage, myogenic cells started to colonize the inner layer anteriorly (Zhao and Dhoot, 2000b), and this corresponded to downregulation of Hgf expression in the outer layer
evidence: This is demonstrated by in situ hybridization shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E-E''.

claim: The smooth muscle layers of the esophagus are the major source of Hgf for anterior-posterior migration of myogenic progenitors.
source: Altogether, our data indicate that the smooth muscle layers of the esophagus are the major source of Hgf for anterior-posterior migration of myogenic progenitors.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the in situ hybridization data.

claim: Met was expressed at high levels anteriorly in Isl1-derived mGFP+ myogenic cells, and also in luminal epithelial cells.
source: In turn, Met was expressed at high levels anteriorly in Isl1-derived mGFP+ myogenic cells, and also in luminal epithelial cells
evidence: This is demonstrated by in situ hybridization shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1G,H.

claim: The levels of Met transcript in mGFP+ cells were heterogeneous.
source: However, the levels of Met transcript in mGFP+ cells were heterogeneous.
evidence: This is an observation from the in situ hybridization data.

claim: 34% of mGFP+ cells were Myod+/Myog+ and 74% of these Myod+/Myog+ cells had low levels of Met transcript (score 0 and 1).
source: Co-immunostaining with Myod and Myog antibodies to detect differentiating myogenic cells, revealed that 34% of mGFP+ cells were Myod+/Myog+ and that 74% of these Myod+/Myog+ cells had low levels of Met transcript (score 0 and 1;
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification shown in Figure 5D,E.

source: Conversely, 91% of the Myod-/Myog- cells, expressed high levels of Met (score 3 and 4)

claim: Laryngeal muscles that also originate from the posterior pharyngeal arches are unaffected in Met mutants.
source: Surprisingly, laryngeal muscles that also originate from the posterior pharyngeal arches are unaffected in Met mutants, thereby uncoupling the genetic requirements between ontogenically similar groups of CPM-derived muscles.
evidence: This is a key finding from the Met mutant analysis.

claim: Isl1 acts cell-autonomously during ESM formation at fetal stages.
source: Here, by means of chimeric analysis, we show that Isl1-null ES cells are specifically excluded from the ESM indicating that Isl1 acts cell-autonomously during ESM formation at fetal stages
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the chimera experiments.

claim: In the trunk, Hgf is first expressed adjacent to somites, and subsequently along the migratory route and at target sites in limb connective tissue.
source: In the trunk, Hgf is first expressed adjacent to somites, and subsequently along the migratory route and at target sites in limb connective tissue (Dietrich et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Dietrich et al., 1999.

claim: HGF is mainly localized in smooth muscle cells in endodermal organs including the stomach and esophagus.
source: This finding is in agreement with a recent study showing that HGF is mainly localized in smooth muscle cells in endodermal organs including the stomach and esophagus (Jangphattananont et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Jangphattananont et al., 2019.

claim: In the limb, Hgf transcripts retreat in the subectodermal region, but a proximo-distal Hgf transcript gradient along the migration route of Met+ myogenic progenitors is not clearly observed.
source: In the limb, Hgf transcripts retreat in the subectodermal region, but a proximo-distal Hgf transcript gradient along the migration route of Met+ myogenic progenitors is not clearly observed (Birchmeier and Gherardi, 1998; Bladt et al., 1995; Dietrich et al., 1999; Yang et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: A gradient for migration might be established by a decrease of Hgf source anteriorly, given the decrease in size and number of smooth muscle cells that occurs cranially from fetal stages.
source: Thus, it is possible that a gradient for migration is established by a decrease of Hgf source anteriorly, given the decrease in size and number of smooth muscle cells that occurs cranially from fetal stages (Zhao and Dhoot, 2000a).
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observed Hgf dynamics.

claim: The fate of smooth muscle cells has been debated, nevertheless a combination of cell loss and distal compaction of smooth muscle cells, appear to be contributing factors.
source: The fate of smooth muscle cells has been debated, nevertheless a combination of cell loss and distal compaction of smooth muscle cells, appear to be contributing factors (Krauss et al., 2016; Rishniw et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: HGF bioavailability depends on a number of factors including HGF activators and inhibitors that exert essential roles during embryonic development and muscle regeneration.
source: HGF bioavailability depends on a number of factors including HGF activators and inhibitors that exert essential roles during embryonic development and muscle regeneration (Rodgers et al., 2017; Sisson et al., 2009; Tanaka et al., 2005; van Adelsberg et al., 2001)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Heparin sulfate proteoglycans can enhance MET/HGF signaling.

claim: It has been proposed that a prolonged interaction between MET and HGF may be required to prevent cell re-aggregation, thereby maintaining cell motility and preventing expression of the MRFs.
source: It has been proposed that a prolonged interaction between MET and HGF may be required to prevent cell re-aggregation, thereby maintaining cell motility and preventing expression of the MRFs (Dietrich et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Dietrich et al., 1999.

claim: The first obvious deficiency observed in MetD/D embryos is seen at the time Isl1+ progenitors colonize the smooth muscle scaffold (by E14.5).
source: The first obvious deficiency observed in MetD/D embryos is seen at the time Isl1+ progenitors colonize the smooth muscle scaffold (by E14.5).
evidence: This is an observation from the Met mutant analysis.

claim: MET/HGF signaling might have a role in maintenance of the undifferentiated state of migratory muscle progenitors to allow continuous progression of the myogenic front.
source: Thus, MET/HGF signaling might have a role in maintenance of the undifferentiated state of migratory muscle progenitors to allow continuous progression of the myogenic front.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the Met mutant phenotype and explant culture results.

claim: It has been shown that precocious expression of MRFs in dermomyotomal muscle progenitors prevents their migration into limb buds.
source: However, it has been shown that precocious expression of MRFs in dermomyotomal muscle progenitors prevents their migration into limb buds (Bonnet et al., 2010)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bonnet et al., 2010.

claim: Application of HGF results in reduction of Myod expression.

claim: During limb muscle development, the Met receptor was reported to be under the direct transcriptional regulation of Pax3.
source: During limb muscle development, the Met receptor was reported to be under the direct transcriptional regulation of Pax3 (Epstein et al., 1996).

claim: ESM development requires MET/HGF signaling in a Pax3-independent context.
source: Interestingly, ESM development requires MET/HGF signaling in a Pax3-independent context.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observations in the manuscript.

claim: Pax3 and its paralog Pax7 have partially redundant functions in muscle progenitors.
source: Pax3 and its paralog Pax7 have partially redundant functions in muscle progenitors (Relaix et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Relaix et al., 2006.

claim: Common Pax3/Pax7 binding sites are found in Met regulatory regions in adult limb primary myoblasts.
source: Given that common Pax3/Pax7 binding sites are found in Met regulatory regions in adult limb primary myoblasts (Soleimani et al., 2012), Pax7 could exert such a role in ESM progenitors.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Soleimani et al., 2012.

claim: Pax7 knockout mice develop megaesophagus postnatally with striated muscle present in an abnormally proximal position.
source: Interestingly, Pax7 knockout mice develop megaesophagus postnatally with striated muscle present in an abnormally proximal position (Chihara et al., 2015).

source: Interestingly, Isl1-Lhx3 fusion protein was shown to induce Met expression in motor neurons (Lee et al., 2012).

claim: Several putative Lhx binding sites including consensus Isl1-binding sites (cTAATg) were identified by in silico analysis of Met promoter elements.
source: Intriguingly, several putative Lhx binding sites including consensus Isl1-binding sites (cTAATg) were identified by in silico analysis of Met promoter elements using matinspector (Cartharius et al., 2005) (data not shown).

claim: The myogenic front in the Pax7 knockout esophagus is localized more posteriorly than what was observed in Met-null embryos.
source: The myogenic front in the Pax7 knockout esophagus is localized more posteriorly than what we observed in Met-null embryos (Chihara et al., 2015).

source: Head muscles derived from the second pharyngeal arch and giving rise to branchiomeric facial muscles (orbicularis oculi, buccinator, platysma) appear either strongly reduced or absent, while first arch-derived masticatory (masseter, temporalis) and extraocular muscles are present in MetD/D mutants (Prunotto et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Prunotto et al., 2004.
